name: Battle of Crécy
info: An English army under Edward III, standing on a hillside near Crécy-en-Ponthieu in northern France, beat off repeated attacks by a much larger French army under Philip VI in 1346, during the Hundred Years' War, and went on to take Calais.

facts.date: 26 August 1346, with the fighting continuing late into the night and a further clash the next morning
facts.place: A sloping hillside at Crécy-en-Ponthieu, with Wadicourt on the English left and Crécy and the River Maye on the right, in Ponthieu in northern France
facts.sides: England under King Edward III, with the Prince of Wales and the earls of Northampton, Warwick and Arundel, perhaps 7,000 to 15,000 men by modern estimates; France under King Philip VI, with Charles of Alençon, Rudolph of Lorraine and Louis of Blois, by consensus substantially larger, at least twice and perhaps three times the English by Clifford Rogers's estimate
facts.outcome: The English held their position through repeated French attacks and suffered very few losses, while the French lost heavily, among them King John of Bohemia and Count Charles of Alençon. Philip left the field near midnight.

t: The English chose and prepared the ground: a sloping hillside with its flanks protected, pits dug in front, dismounted men-at-arms in the centre and longbowmen on the flanks, so that the French had to charge uphill.

Estimates of the French army run from about 72,000 or 120,000 in two chronicles to a modern view of at least twice and perhaps three times the English, and the same sources differ on the English as well, from 7,000 to 15,000.
The English laid siege to Calais, which fell eleven months later and stayed in English hands for two hundred years, and the battle established the longbow as a dominant weapon in Western Europe.
dyk: Each English archer was issued two more quivers on the morning of the battle, making 72 arrows per man, and modern historians suggest that half a million arrows could have been shot.
ev: Philip VI's Great Council takes back the lands Edward III holds in France, which marks the start of the Hundred Years' War
A French army under John, Duke of Normandy, marches on Gascony and besieges Aiguillon
The English land at Saint-Vaast-la-Hougue in Normandy and march south, storming Caen on 26 July
The English reach within 2 miles of Paris, then turn north and cross the Somme at the ford of Blanchetaque
The French attack the English position at Crécy-en-Ponthieu, and the Genoese crossbowmen are driven off by the longbowmen
French cavalry charges are broken until nearly midnight, and Philip leaves the field
French forces still arriving are charged by the English, now mounted, and pursued for miles
Calais falls to the English after a siege of eleven months

sections.background:
Since the Norman Conquest of 1066, English monarchs had held titles and lands within France, which made them vassals of the kings of France. After a series of disagreements between Philip VI of France and Edward III of England, Philip's Great Council in Paris agreed on 24 May 1337 that the lands Edward held in France should be taken back into Philip's hands, on the grounds that Edward was in breach of his obligations as a vassal. This marked the start of the Hundred Years' War, which was to last 116 years.

Eight years of intermittent, expensive and inconclusive warfare followed. Edward campaigned three times in northern France to no effect, and Gascony was left almost entirely to its own devices. In 1345 Henry, Earl of Derby, led a campaign through Gascony, defeated two large French armies at Bergerac and Auberoche and captured more than 100 towns and fortifications. In March 1346 a French army of between 15,000 and 20,000 under John, Duke of Normandy, the son and heir of Philip VI, marched on Gascony and besieged the town of Aiguillon.

Derby, now Lancaster, sent an urgent appeal for help to Edward, who was bound by his indenture with Lancaster to rescue him if he were attacked by overwhelming numbers. Edward raised a fresh army and assembled more than 700 vessels to carry it, the largest English fleet to that date. The French relied on their navy to guard northern France, and that reliance proved misplaced.
sections.forces:
The English army was made up almost exclusively of English and Welsh soldiers, with a handful of disaffected Normans and a few German mercenaries, probably no more than 150 foreigners in all. Its exact size and make-up are not known. Modern historians have estimated it at from 7,000 to 15,000. Andrew Ayton suggests around 14,000, Clifford Rogers 15,000, and Jonathan Sumption, going by the carrying capacity of the transport fleet, 7,000 to 10,000. Up to a thousand men were convicted felons serving on the promise of a pardon. The men-at-arms fought dismounted, and the army also had small guns, ribauldequins and bombards in unknown numbers.

Edward drew up three battles in a column on a sloping hillside facing south-east. The Prince of Wales, aided by the earls of Northampton and Warwick, commanded the vanguard with 800 men-at-arms, 2,000 archers and 1,000 foot soldiers. The Earl of Arundel led a second battle with 800 men-at-arms and 1,200 archers, and the King held the reserve with 700 men-at-arms and 2,000 archers. The flanks were secured by Wadicourt, Crécy and the River Maye, pits were dug in front, and the baggage was circled behind.

The size of the French army is even less certain. The two chroniclers who give totals say 72,000 or 120,000, figures historians call exaggerated. Rogers estimates that it was at least twice as large as the English and perhaps three times. By modern estimates 8,000 mounted men-at-arms formed its core, with two to six thousand Genoese crossbowmen and a large, indeterminate number of common infantry. The Genoese, under Antonio Doria and Carlo Grimaldi, formed the vanguard, followed by Charles of Alençon with King John of Bohemia, then Rudolph of Lorraine and Louis of Blois, with Philip commanding the rearguard.
sections.course:
Around noon on 26 August French scouts came in sight of the English. A council of war advised attacking the next day, as the army was tired from a 12-mile march, but the French attacked later the same afternoon. It is unclear whether this was Philip's choice or whether too many knights pressed forward. His plan was for the crossbowmen to disorder the English infantry so that the mounted men-at-arms could break in. As the French advanced with the oriflamme unfurled, a sudden rainstorm broke. The English archers unstrung their bows. Some historians hold that the rain weakened the Genoese strings, others that leather coverings protected them.

The longbowmen outranged the crossbowmen and shot more than three times as fast, and the Genoese were without their pavises, which were still with the baggage. The Genoese were rapidly defeated and fled. French knights following them hacked at them as they retreated, and the leading battle fell into disarray. Alençon's battle then charged, disordered by the fleeing Italians, the mud, the uphill slope and the pits, and broken up further by the English archers, whose arrows killed or wounded the unarmoured horses in large numbers.

Fresh French cavalry repeated the charge over ground littered with dead and wounded horses and men. The Prince of Wales was reported beaten to his knees at one point, and Edward sent help from his reserve. How many times the French charged is disputed, but the attacks continued late into the night, each ending in fierce fighting and a French retreat. Blind King John of Bohemia tied his bridle to those of his attendants and rode into the twilight, and all were killed. Philip had two horses killed under him, took an arrow in the jaw and left the field near midnight.
sections.aftermath:
The English slept where they had fought. The next morning substantial French forces were still arriving. The English men-at-arms, now mounted, charged them and pursued them for miles, and the losses in that clash were reported as several thousand, including the Duke of Lorraine. Estimates of the dead on the second day run from 2,000 to, according to Edward III himself, 4,000. Some sources say Edward ordered that no prisoners be taken, but there is no record of any until the next day.

All contemporary sources agree that English losses were very low. Three or four men-at-arms and a small number of the rank and file were reported dead, forty in all by a roll-call after the battle, though some modern historians think it too few and put the English dead at around three hundred. English heralds counted the bodies of 1,542 French noble men-at-arms, perhaps not including those who died the next day. The dead included one king, nine princes, ten counts, a duke, an archbishop and a bishop.

No reliable figures exist for the common soldiers. Jean Le Bel estimated 15,000 to 16,000 French dead and Froissart 30,000 killed or captured, while Alfred Burne guessed 10,000 infantry, for a total of 12,000 French dead. Edward then laid siege to Calais, which fell after eleven months, the battle having crippled the French army's ability to relieve it. Duke John had left Aiguillon on 20 August but did not arrive in time to change the course of events in the north.
sections.sources:
The battle is known from chroniclers writing in its time. Froissart wrote more than one version of his Chronicles, and his estimates of the English army differ so much between them that the third more than doubles the first. Jean Le Bel gives a figure for the French dead, an Italian chronicler gives his own totals for the French army, and the account of the hand-to-hand fighting as murderous and without pity comes from a contemporary. The financial records of the French campaign are lost, which is why the size of the French army cannot be fixed. English heralds counted the noble dead, and iron balls compatible with bombard ammunition have been recovered from the site.

Much is disputed. Historians differ on the size of both armies, on whether the rain weakened the Genoese crossbows, on how many casualties the Genoese suffered, on whether Edward gave an order to take no prisoners, on how many times the French charged, on how many English died, and on why Philip left the field. The sources also leave unclear whether the French attack was Philip's deliberate choice.
sections.legacy:
Clifford Rogers calls the result a total victory for the English, and Andrew Ayton calls it unprecedented and a devastating military humiliation for the French. Jonathan Sumption considers it a political catastrophe for the French Crown. The battle was reported to the English parliament on 13 September in glowing terms, as a sign of divine favour and a justification for the huge cost of the war to date. Rogers writes that the English benefitted from superior organisation, cohesion and leadership and from the indiscipline of the French. Ayton writes that England's international reputation as a military power was established in an evening's hard fighting.

Calais gave the English a port and a foothold in northern France that they held until 1558, more than two centuries. The battle established the effectiveness of the longbow as a dominant weapon on the Western European battlefield, and English and Welsh archers served as mercenaries in Italy in significant numbers and some as far afield as Hungary. The historian Joseph Dahmus includes Crécy in his Seven Decisive Battles of the Middle Ages.

summary: At Crécy on 26 August 1346 Edward III's English army, drawn up on a prepared hillside, beat off repeated attacks by a much larger French army under Philip VI and lost very few men. The English then took Calais, which they held until 1558.

Henri de Wailly, Crécy 1346: Anatomy of a Battle (Blandford Press, 1987)

notes: Sizes: the English figures are modern estimates from 7,000 to 15,000 (Ayton about 14,000, Rogers 15,000, Sumption 7,000-10,000); the French have no reliable figure. I kept Rogers's 'at least twice, perhaps three times' and the two chroniclers' 72,000 and 120,000 as the article gives them.

The article says the English were 'rested and well-fed' and in high morale; left out for length. Also left out: equipment of both sides, the Count of Savoy's march, the Flemings' failed expedition, the Caen sack (only the date is in ev), and the longbow penetration study of 2017.

The article gives the date of the fighting as 26 August with the battle continuing late into the night; the next-morning clash is on the 27th by implication only, so ev uses 27 August 1346 as the day after.

The article has no sources section; the sources paragraph uses only what it says of chroniclers (Froissart, Le Bel, an Italian chronicler), the lost financial records, the heralds' count and the iron balls found at the site, and then lists the disputes it names.
Aftermath: Duke John's march north from Aiguillon on 20 August is in the Prelude; I used it as a short closing note.
ev entry 'August 1346' compresses the march to the Seine, the turn north and the Blanchetaque crossing (24-25 August in the article's narrative: the night of 24 August).
The Battle section of the article says the second day's losses were 'reported as several thousand'; the Casualties section gives 2,000 to 4,000; both used.
